claims.text: RFC 9309 frames robots.txt as rules crawlers are requested to honor, and says those rules are not a form of access authorization.
acceptable_patterns: not a form of access authorization

evidence_passages.text: RFC 9309 defines robots.txt as a protocol for crawler behavior and expressly says it is not access authorization.

"These rules are not a form of access authorization." (Section 1.3) ... "crawlers are requested to honor when accessing URIs" (Section 1.3), framing the rules as guidance rather than mandatory enforcement.

claims.text: Google documentation similarly treats robots.txt as traffic management rather than enforcement: it says robots.txt cannot enforce crawler behavior, is not by itself a way to keep pages out of Google, and disallowed URLs can still appear in search results.
acceptable_patterns: not a way to keep pages out of Google
disallowed URLs can still appear in search results

evidence_passages.text: Google’s documentation is similar: it says robots.txt is mainly for managing crawler traffic, “cannot enforce crawler behavior,” is not a way to keep pages out of Google by itself, and disallowed URLs can still appear in search results.

claims.text: Within standards work, one W3C Community Group document defines a separate TDM Reservation Protocol capable of expressing reservation of rights under EU copyright law and says it is not a W3C Standard.
acceptable_patterns: capable of expressing the reservation of rights

evidence_passages.text: The W3C Community Group’s TDM Reservation Protocol instead defines a separate protocol “capable of expressing the reservation of rights” for text and data mining under EU copyright law, and its status page says it is not a W3C Standard.

claims.text: The same W3C Community Group later said using robots.txt as a search opt-in is only a complementary solution, that this complementarity remains subject to interpretation, and that a more explicit signal could be more secure.
acceptable_patterns: more explicit signal could be more secure

evidence_passages.text: The same W3C Community Group later wrote that using robots.txt as a search opt-in is only a “complementary solution,” that this complementarity “remains subject to interpretation,” and that a more explicit signal could be more secure.

claims.text: Standards participants also disagree about legal significance for AI uses: an IETF draft proposes robots.txt carry usage preferences, while EDRLab meeting notes say an AI-Pref signal in robots.txt is logically sufficient to express a reservation of rights under EU CDSM Article 4.
acceptable_patterns: logically sufficient to express a reservation of rights

evidence_passages.text: Meanwhile, an active IETF draft proposes updating RFC 9309 so robots.txt can carry “usage preferences”.
EDRLab’s notes from the IETF AI-Pref meeting say the presence of an AI-Pref signal in robots.txt is “logically sufficient to express a reservation of rights” under EU CDSM Article 4.

claims.text: Crawler operators use mixed language too: Google says its common crawlers always obey robots.txt rules, while OpenAI advertiser guidance says robots.txt tells crawlers whether they are permitted to access parts of a site.
acceptable_patterns: permitted to access parts of a site

evidence_passages.text: Google says its common crawlers “always obey robots.txt rules when crawling automatically,” and its `Google-Extended` token lets publishers manage whether crawled content may be used for Gemini training and grounding.

OpenAI’s advertiser guidance is even stronger permission language: it says robots.txt tells crawlers whether they are “permitted” to access parts of a site and that crawling stops if access is disallowed.

claims.text: Publishers are split as well: Medium describes robots.txt as where it tells bots what they are and are not allowed to crawl, but the same post also says robots.txt is not a legally binding arrangement and is a voluntary technical standard.
acceptable_patterns: what they are and are not allowed to crawl

evidence_passages.text: Medium’s official blog says bots crawl public-web content by default, describes robots.txt as the place where Medium tells bots what they are and are not allowed to crawl, and frames search crawling as a trade of consent, credit, and compensation.
But the same Medium post also says robots.txt “isn’t a legally binding arrangement,” is a “voluntary technical standard,” and depends on actors respecting it.

rejected_claims.text: robots.txt universally grants permission to crawl.
rejected_claims.reason: Contradicted by the supplied RFC 9309 evidence saying robots.txt rules are not a form of access authorization.

rejected_claims.text: Standards participants agree that robots.txt is only a preference signal with no claimed legal significance.
rejected_claims.reason: Contradicted by supplied evidence about TDM reservation protocols, the AI-Pref draft, and EDRLab notes about reservation of rights.

rejected_claims.text: robots.txt alone creates binding legal duties everywhere.
rejected_claims.reason: Overly broad and unsupported; the supplied evidence explicitly says there is not good evidence of a universal rule.

rejected_claims.text: All crawler operators describe robots.txt the same way.
rejected_claims.reason: Contradicted by supplied evidence showing both advisory language and stronger permission language.

rejected_claims.text: Publishers uniformly treat robots.txt as legally binding.
rejected_claims.reason: Contradicted by the supplied Medium evidence calling it a voluntary technical standard and not a legally binding arrangement.
